segments.caption: Why does the casino never lose? The law of large numbers.
The tiny edge, a coin experiment, the law, real-life uses, and the gambler's mistake. Save this one!
Every night in Goa, someone walks out of a casino with lakhs in their pocket.
Yet the casino itself never loses. Not this month. Not this year.
Is the game rigged? No. It's just maths.
Take roulette. The wheel has 37 pockets: 18 red, 18 black, and one green zero.
Bet on red: 18 out of 37. A 48.6% chance.
The casino wins the other 51.4%. That one green zero gives the house an edge of just 2.7%.
So for every Rs 100 bet, the casino keeps about Rs 2.70, on average.

scenes.title: One player vs millions of spins

segments.caption: For you, one night is pure luck. You might win five spins in a row and go home rich.
But the casino isn't playing one night. It's playing millions of spins. And over millions of spins, luck stops mattering.
Let's prove it with a fair coin. The true chance of heads is 50%.
10 flips: 7 heads. 70%. Way off.
100 flips: 54%. Closer.
That's the law of large numbers.
As the number of trials grows, the average result gets closer and closer to the expected value.
In interview language: the sample mean converges to the population mean as the sample size grows.
Say the casino takes 10 lakh bets of Rs 100 in a year. That's Rs 10 crore bet.
The edge says it keeps 2.7%: Rs 27 lakh.
And with that many bets, its real profit lands between about Rs 25 and 29 lakh, almost every time.
Short term, it's luck. Long term, it's maths.
This law runs real life too.
Insurance: nobody knows which driver will crash, but across 10 lakh drivers, the company knows almost exactly how many will. That sets your premium.
Cricket: a batting average after 3 innings means nothing. After 100 innings, it shows who the player really is.
Ratings: 5 stars from 3 reviews? Don't trust it. 4.6 stars from 5,000 reviews is the real picture.
But here's the trap. After five reds in a row, people bet on black: it's due.
It isn't. The wheel has no memory. Every spin is still 48.6%.
The average evens out, not because the wheel corrects itself, but because millions of new spins drown out the old ones. That's the gambler's fallacy.
So remember: small samples can lie. Large samples tell the truth.
Save this, and send it to the friend who says "this time I'll definitely win."
